ai.literal: By sweet words, affection having mingled, deceit free from being, [is] the word from the mouth of those who have realized the ultimate truth.
ai.translation: A sweet word is speech from the mouth of those who have realized the ultimate truth, mingled with love and free from all deceit.
ai.modern: மெய்ப்பொருளை உணர்ந்தவர்களின் வாயிலிருந்து வரும் சொற்கள், அன்போடு கலந்து, வஞ்சனை இல்லாத இனிய சொற்களாக இருக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true nature of sweet speech. It states that genuine sweet words are those spoken by people who have realized the ultimate truth of life. Their speech is naturally infused with sincere love and affection, and is completely free from any form of deceit or hypocrisy. Thus, true sweetness in language is not mere flattery, but a reflection of inner realization and heartfelt compassion.

ai.literal: With a delighted heart, than giving, is indeed better, with a delighted face, to be one who speaks sweet words, if one can be.
ai.translation: If one can be a person who speaks sweet words with a cheerful face, that is indeed better than giving gifts with a glad heart.
ai.modern: மனம் மகிழ்ந்து கொடுப்பதைக் காட்டிலும், முகம் மலர்ந்து இனிய சொற்களைப் பேசுபவனாக இருக்கப் பெற்றால் அதுவே மிகச் சிறந்ததாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the virtue of charity with the virtue of pleasant speech. While giving gifts with a glad heart is highly praised, the poet asserts that speaking sweet words with a cheerful, welcoming face is even better. The words 'akan' (heart) and 'mukaṉ' (face) are contrasted to show that internal joy must manifest as external warmth. The repetition of 'amarntu' (delighting) emphasizes that both the giving and the speaking must be done with genuine pleasure, but the latter has a greater everyday value.

ai.literal: With a face being pleased, sweetly looking, with the heart arising sweet words, of such a nature indeed is virtue.
ai.translation: To look at others with a cheerful, welcoming face, and to speak sweet words that flow sincerely from the heart—this indeed is the nature of true virtue.
ai.modern: மகிழ்ச்சியான முகத்தோடு அன்புடன் நோக்கி, உள்ளத்திலிருந்து வரும் இனிய சொற்களைக் கூறுவதே உண்மையான அறமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the essence of virtue not as grand, difficult deeds, but as simple, everyday interpersonal warmth. It highlights two essential components: the external expression and the internal sincerity. First, one must look at others with a pleased, welcoming face and a sweet gaze. Second, the sweet words spoken must genuinely arise from the heart, rather than being mere empty flattery. The poet concludes that this combination of a warm look and sincere, sweet speech is itself the very nature of virtue.

ai.literal: Misery-causing poverty will not exist for those who speak pleasure-giving sweet words towards anyone.
ai.translation: Poverty, which brings misery, will never come to those who speak sweet words that bring joy to everyone.
ai.modern: எல்லாரிடமும் இன்பம் தரும் இனிய சொற்களைப் பேசுபவர்களிடம், துன்பத்தைத் தரும் வறுமை அணுகாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet links pleasant speech with the removal of life's hardships. The word 'துவ்வாமை' refers to poverty or destitution, which is described as 'துன்புறூஉம்' (that which causes misery). Conversely, 'இன்சொல்' (sweet words) are described as 'இன்புறூஉம்' (that which brings joy) to 'யார்மாட்டும்' (everyone). The poet asserts that those who consistently speak kindly to all will be spared from the suffering of poverty, as their pleasant nature naturally attracts goodwill, support, and prosperity.

ai.literal: Being one who has humility and one who speaks sweet words is the ornament to a person; other things are not.
ai.translation: Humility and pleasant words are the only true ornaments for a person; all other external adornments are not real ornaments.
ai.modern: ஒருவனுக்குப் பணிவு உடையவனாகவும் இனிய சொற்களைப் பேசுபவனாகவும் விளங்குவதே உண்மையான அணிகலனாகும்; மற்றவை எல்லாம் உண்மையான அணிகலன்கள் அல்ல.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines what constitutes true ornamentation for a human being. The author states that possessing humility and speaking sweet, gentle words are the only genuine ornaments a person can wear. External decorations, such as jewels or fine clothing, are dismissed as not being true ornaments. The inner virtues of character and speech are elevated above physical adornments, emphasizing that moral beauty is far superior to material display.

ai.literal: Evils having diminished, virtue will increase, good things having sought, pleasant words if one speaks.
ai.translation: If one seeks to do good and speaks pleasant words, their sins will diminish and virtue will grow.
ai.modern: நன்மையானவற்றை விரும்பி, இனிமையான சொற்களைப் பேசினால், பாவங்கள் தேய்ந்து அழியும்; அறம் பெருகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the transformative power of kind speech. When a person actively seeks out what is good (நல்லவை நாடி) and speaks sweet, pleasant words (இனிய சொலின்), it brings about a dual effect. Their vices and past sins (அல்லவை) gradually wear away and diminish (தேய), while their righteousness and moral virtue (அறம்) grow and flourish (பெருகும்). The poet shows that pleasant speech is not just a social courtesy but a powerful practice that purifies one's character.

ai.literal: Words that do not deviate from courtesy, yielding benefit, will yield pleasantness and produce virtue.
ai.translation: Words that do not deviate from courtesy, while yielding fruitful benefits, will produce pleasantness and yield lasting virtue.
ai.modern: நற்பண்பிலிருந்து விலகாமல், நன்மையைத் தந்து, இன்பத்தையும் அறத்தையும் தருவது இனிய சொற்கள் ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the profound impact of speaking sweet words that are rooted in good character. Words that do not deviate from courtesy and bring practical benefit have a dual effect. They produce immediate pleasantness or harmony and yield long-term moral virtue. Thus, true sweet speech is not mere flattery, but a virtuous act that benefits both the speaker and the listener.

ai.literal: Sweet words free from meanness will give happiness both in the next life and in this life.
ai.translation: Sweet speech, free from all meanness, yields happiness both in this life and in the life to come.
ai.modern: பிறருக்குத் துன்பம் தராத இனிய சொற்கள், ஒருவருக்கு இப்பிறப்பிலும் மறுபிறப்பிலும் இன்பத்தைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the dual benefit of speaking sweet words that are devoid of meanness or the intent to cause harm. Such pleasant speech does not just bring joy and harmonious relationships in the present life, but also accumulates spiritual merit that brings happiness in the next life. The key term 'சிறுமையுவு நீங்கிய' (traditionally 'சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய') emphasizes that true sweet words must be completely free from pettiness, malice, or deceit. Thus, gentle and kind words are a source of eternal happiness.

ai.literal: Sweet word yielding pleasure he who sees, why indeed harsh word uttering?
ai.translation: When one sees that sweet words yield pleasure, why on earth does he still utter harsh words?
ai.modern: இனிய சொற்கள் நன்மையைத் தருவதைக் கண்டும் ஒருவன் கடுஞ்சொற்களைப் பேசுவது ஏனோ?
ai.explanation: The couplet questions the logic of human behavior regarding speech. A person can clearly observe that speaking sweet words ('இன்சொல்') brings happiness and positive outcomes ('இனிது') to both the speaker and the listener. Knowing this, it is foolish and inexplicable ('எவன்கொலோ') that one would still choose to utter harsh, painful words ('வன்சொல்'). The poet highlights that choosing kind speech is a matter of simple common sense.

ai.literal: Pleasant words while existing, speaking harsh words is like choosing unripe fruit while ripe fruit is present.
ai.translation: Speaking harsh words when pleasant words are available is like choosing to eat unripe fruit when ripe fruit is at hand.
ai.modern: இனிய சொற்கள் இருக்கும்போது கடுமையான சொற்களைப் பேசுவது, பழுத்த பழங்கள் இருக்கும்போது பச்சைக் காய்களைத் தேர்ந்தெடுத்து உண்பதற்கு ஒப்பானது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a simple yet powerful analogy to highlight the foolishness of using harsh language. The poet compares pleasant words to sweet, ripe fruits and harsh words to bitter, unripe fruits. When both options are available, choosing to speak harshly is as senseless as choosing to eat sour, unripe fruit when delicious ripe fruit is readily available. The word 'kavarntu' here means choosing or taking with desire, emphasizing the active, foolish choice of the speaker.
